description: We are a team of four developers from Juiz de Fora, Brazil, tackling the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. Our goal is to merge more than two decades of satellite fire data into a single, consistent record, correcting the differences between the two sensors so that real changes in burning activity aren’t confused with changes in technology.
summary: Brasa turns two generations of NASA fire satellites into one consistent fire history of the Brazilian Pantanal, from 2003 to today. MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see fire very differently, so joining them naively makes fire seem to jump in 2012. We count fire on a common grid of ~5 km² H3 hexagons and convert older MODIS counts into VIIRS equivalents with one calibrated factor per calendar month. Tested on years left out of calibration, the conversion lands close to the real VIIRS count (2019: +12.5%; 2020: −4.2%), with no jump at the sensor switch, and our year ranking matches INPE's reference series (Spearman 0.98). Anyone can draw an area on the map and get, in seconds, its fire days per year, a year-by-month calendar, how the latest month compares with its own history, a density map and a CSV of the raw NASA detections. The Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland, had its worst fire year of the series in 2020 and another severe one in 2024: ranchers, park managers, journalists and researchers need a long, comparable record for their own area.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Brasa is an open web app. Draw a polygon or a rectangle on the map of the Brazilian Pantanal (or click "Whole Brazilian Pantanal"), pick a period, and get a dashboard of that area's fire history from January 2003 to the latest data:

- total fire days, the worst year, and the peak month next to the usual peak month;

- a year × month fire calendar;

- fire days per year;

- how the latest month compares with the same month in every past year (times the median, and its percentile);

- a density map of H3 hexagons;

- a CSV of the original NASA detections, each with the harmonization factor applied to it.

No login, nothing to install. English, Portuguese and Spanish, light and dark themes, colour-blind-safe palettes.

HOW IT WORKS: HARMONIZING MODIS AND VIIRS

Our approach is inspired by the GFED5 near-real-time extension (Chen et al., 2026, Earth Syst. Sci. Data), which links VIIRS and MODIS-based fire records through scaling factors calibrated over the 2012–2022 overlap. We adapt that idea to a local, user-drawn scale: H3 cell-days instead of 0.25° grid cells, one factor per calendar month, and conversion of older MODIS counts into VIIRS equivalents.

1. One reference satellite per sensor: MODIS on Aqua (2003–2011 in the series) and VIIRS on Suomi NPP (from 2012). Their daytime overpasses are minutes apart (~13:30 local time).

2. Filters: vegetation fires only (type = 0), MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal or high confidence, inside the IBGE Pantanal biome boundary plus a 2 km buffer.

3. Cell-days, not detections: H3 hexagons at resolution 7 (~5 km²). A cell-day counts 1 if a sensor saw at least one fire there that day. A VIIRS pixel is about 7 times smaller than a MODIS pixel, so counting detections exaggerates the gap: in 2020 the VIIRS/MODIS ratio was 7.2 in detections but 2.7 in cell-days.

4. One factor per calendar month: R_m = VIIRS cell-days ÷ Aqua daytime cell-days, calibrated on 2012–2018 and 2021, with 2019 and 2020 held out for testing. Factors range from 2.61 (August: big dry-season fires that both sensors see) to 4.67 (February: small fires that mostly only VIIRS catches).

5. Before 2012, each Aqua cell-day is multiplied by R_m; from 2012, real VIIRS cell-days are used. One unit everywhere: fire days per ~5 km² cell, VIIRS equivalent.

VALIDATION

Predicting the held-out years from MODIS alone gives +12.5% (2019) and −4.2% (2020) against the real VIIRS count, monthly correlation ≥ 0.99, the correct peak month in both years, and no jump between 2011 and 2012. We compared five variants (monthly factor with Aqua daytime only, with Aqua day + night, separate day/night factors, and two log regressions) and kept the one with the lowest average error that is also the simplest to explain. The resulting year ranking matches INPE's reference-satellite series for the Pantanal (Spearman 0.98, same five worst years).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- A long, comparable fire record for any area someone cares about (a ranch, a park, a watershed), not only states or municipalities.

- One series across two sensor generations, so "is this year worse than usual?" has an honest answer back to 2003.

- Open and reproducible: the CSV carries the raw NASA detections and the factor applied to each, so anyone can check or redo the numbers.

- Intended users: ranchers, park managers, fire brigades, journalists, researchers and public agencies working in the Pantanal.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- We change the question before calibrating: instead of comparing raw detections, we ask "did this 5 km² hexagon burn on this day?". That alone removes most of the resolution gap between the two sensors.

- A factor per calendar month, not one for the whole year, captures that the sensors disagree differently in the dry and wet seasons.

- The heavy science runs once, offline; each click on the map is a quick lookup over pre-computed cell-days, so the harmonized history of any drawn area appears in seconds.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- False steps in the record: only one satellite per sensor, so no jump appears when Terra, NOAA-20 or NOAA-21 enter or leave the archive.

- Aqua's orbit drift from 2022: those years are not used for calibration.

- Saturation in extreme fire years (the VIIRS/MODIS ratio falls as fire grows): measured, documented, and a log regression kept as plan B.

- Small areas: the app warns when an area is under ~500 km², where yearly numbers are noisier.

- Honest units: we say "fire days per ~5 km² cell" so nobody compares our numbers with INPE's hotspot counts.

- Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, keyboard drawing shortcuts, screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support, two languages.

TOOLS

Python 3.12, pandas, GeoPandas, shapely, pyproj, h3-py, psycopg, FastAPI, Pydantic, pytest, PostgreSQL + PostGIS, Docker, Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, ECharts. Hosting: GitHub (code).

NEXT STEPS

Daily updates from the FIRMS near-real-time feed; carrying the series forward with NOAA-20, calibrated against Suomi NPP with the same method; burned-area estimates; extending to the Bolivian and Paraguayan Pantanal.
